# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The growth of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has been constrained by the need for large-bore vascular access. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), endovascular aneurysm repair, and emerging mitral interventions frequently require sheaths of 14–26 French [1]. Although transfemoral arterial access remains the default, a substantial minority of patients—particularly those with small, calcified, or tortuous iliofemoral vessels—are unsuitable [2]. Alternative routes including transapical, transaortic, transaxillary, and transcarotid access carry their own morbidity [3]. Transcaval access, in which the abdominal aorta is entered from the adjacent inferior vena cava (IVC), has emerged as a percutaneous, fully transvenous strategy for delivering large devices [4].

## Concept and Rationale

The transcaval technique exploits the close anatomic apposition of the infrarenal abdominal aorta and the IVC [5]. An electrified guidewire is advanced from the IVC across the aortic wall under fluoroscopic and often computed tomographic guidance, creating a controlled aortocaval fistula through which a large sheath is delivered [6]. Counterintuitively, bleeding into the retroperitoneum is limited because retroperitoneal pressure exceeds central venous pressure, encouraging blood to decompress back into the vein rather than into the retroperitoneal space [7]. At the conclusion of the procedure, the aortocaval tract is closed, classically with a nitinol occluder device originally designed for ductal or muscular ventricular septal defect closure [8].

## Technique Evolution

The first systematic human experience was reported by Greenbaum and colleagues, who demonstrated feasibility in patients undergoing TAVR who lacked alternative access [9]. Preprocedural planning relies on contrast-enhanced CT to identify a calcium-free target on the aortic wall and a suitable crossing trajectory avoiding lumbar arteries and bowel [10]. Electrosurgical crossing using a guidewire connected to an electrocautery pen has become standard, providing efficient tissue penetration with minimal force [11]. Snaring of the crossing wire in the aorta establishes a through-and-through rail for sheath advancement [12]. Refinements in closure—including dedicated devices and improved sizing algorithms—have reduced residual fistula and bleeding [13].

## Clinical Outcomes

The prospective multicenter Transcaval Access for TAVR study enrolled 100 patients and reported successful transcaval access in 99% and successful aortic closure in 98%, with acceptable rates of major vascular and bleeding complications given the comorbid population [14]. Subsequent registry data confirmed reproducibility across multiple centers [15]. Comparative analyses suggest transcaval access yields outcomes competitive with, and in some series superior to, transthoracic alternatives, with shorter recovery and avoidance of general anesthesia in selected cases [16]. Importantly, persistent aortocaval fistulae are frequently asymptomatic and many close spontaneously, although a minority require percutaneous reintervention [17].

## Complications and Management

The principal concerns are retroperitoneal and intraperitoneal bleeding, hemodynamic instability, and residual fistula [18]. Most bleeding is self-limited, but transfusion and occasional covered-stent or coil intervention may be required [19]. Careful patient selection—avoiding heavily calcified target zones and interposed structures—mitigates risk [20]. Hemodynamic monitoring for high-output fistula is recommended, although clinically significant left-to-right shunting is rare [21]. Centers have developed bailout algorithms incorporating balloon tamponade, covered stents, and surgical backup [22].

## Expanding Indications

Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has been applied to deliver mechanical circulatory support, perform endovascular aneurysm repair, and facilitate transcatheter mitral and tricuspid interventions requiring large delivery systems [23]. The transvenous route is attractive for thoracoabdominal and complex aortic work where conventional arterial access is hostile [24]. As transcatheter mitral valve replacement devices mature, their large profiles make transcaval delivery an appealing investigational pathway [25].

## Comparative Context and Future Directions

Decision-making among alternative-access options should be individualized and informed by multidisciplinary heart-team evaluation and dedicated CT analysis [26]. Studies comparing transcaval with transcarotid and transaxillary approaches highlight tradeoffs in stroke risk, bleeding, and operator familiarity [27]. Dedicated transcaval crossing and closure systems under development promise to standardize the procedure and reduce reliance on off-label hardware [28]. Improvements in imaging fusion and intravascular guidance may further enhance safety [29]. Ongoing prospective evaluation will define long-term durability of aortocaval closure and refine the role of transcaval access within the structural heart armamentarium [30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from an ingenious concept into a validated, reproducible technique for large-bore device delivery in patients without suitable transfemoral arterial access. With careful imaging-based planning and standardized closure, it offers a fully percutaneous, transvenous alternative that broadens treatment eligibility. Continued device innovation and comparative outcome data will solidify its place in structural heart intervention.
